ownership_reason: Only the gold holds each element together with the answer of the set for it: hops 1 and 2 hold the whole list, hops 3 and 4 the moved elements, and none of them consults the set per element. The convention is pinned outside the gold: the facade's javadoc ('If the list contains duplicates, these are removed (first indexed one kept)'); the SetUniqueList(List, Set) constructor ('The set and list must both be correctly initialised to the same elements'); SetUniqueList.addAll(int, Collection) takes the same step (`if (set.add(e)) temp.add(e)`; SetUniqueListTest testAddAll and testIntCollectionAddAll: 'Duplicate element should not be added'); ListOrderedSet.addAll(int, Collection) takes it with the same idiom (`if (contains(e)) continue; collection.add(e); toAdd.add(e);`; ListOrderedSetTest testListAddIndexed); SetUniqueList.add(int, E) adds only when `set.contains(object) == false`. The step is decided by the set itself (SetUniqueList307 in SetUniqueListTest wraps a TreeSet; createSetBasedOnList keeps the set's class), so hops 1-4 and the gold take any Set. A one-line equality pre-filter above the gold (CollectionUtils.filter(list, PredicateUtils.uniquePredicate()) at hop 1, a LinkedHashSet copy at hops 2-4) passes the existing tests with the facade's HashSet but decides by equals/hashCode instead of by the set the hops are documented to fill: for a TreeSet ordered by String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER and the list ["a", "A"] the list keeps both while the set holds one, so the gold's documented contract (list and set initialised to the same elements) stays violated inside every hop's documented domain; at hop 2 it also breaks the documented move of the list's elements. Rebuilding the list from the set after the gold (list.clear(); list.addAll(set)) passes only because a HashSet of small Integers iterates in ascending order, and loses the first-indexed order for other elements.
